title: Forgiveness, Faith, Ten Lepers, and the Coming Kingdom

verses.text: Jesus said to His disciples, "It is inevitable that stumbling blocks will come, but woe to the one through whom they come!
It would be better for him to have a millstone hung around his neck and to be thrown into the sea than to cause one of these little ones to stumble.
Watch yourselves. If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him.
Even if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times returns to say, 'I repent,' you must forgive him."
The apostles said to the Lord, "Increase our faith!"
And the Lord answered, "If you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mulberry tree, 'Be uprooted and planted in the sea,' and it will obey you.
Which of you whose servant comes in from plowing or shepherding in the field will say to him, 'Come at once and sit down to eat'?
Instead, won't he tell him, 'Prepare my meal and dress yourself to serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you may eat and drink'?
Does he thank the servant because he did what he was told?
So you also, when you have done everything commanded of you, should say, 'We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty.'"
While Jesus was on His way to Jerusalem, He was passing between Samaria and Galilee.
As He entered one of the villages, He was met by ten lepers. They stood at a distance
and raised their voices, shouting, "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!"
When Jesus saw them, He said, "Go, show yourselves to the priests." And as they were on their way, they were cleansed.
When one of them saw that he was healed, he came back, praising God in a loud voice.
He fell facedown at Jesus' feet in thanksgiving to Him—and he was a Samaritan.
"Were not all ten cleansed?" Jesus asked. "Where then are the other nine?
Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?"
Then Jesus said to him, "Rise and go; your faith has made you well!"
When asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, Jesus replied, "The kingdom of God will not come with observable signs.
Nor will people say, 'Look, here it is,' or 'There it is.' For you see, the kingdom of God is in your midst."
Then He said to the disciples, "The time is coming when you will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, but you will not see it.
People will tell you, 'Look, there He is!' or 'Look, here He is!' Do not go out or chase after them.
For just as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one end to the other, so will be the Son of Man in His day.
But first He must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.
Just as it was in the days of Noah, so also will it be in the days of the Son of Man:
People were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage, up to the day Noah entered the ark. Then the flood came and destroyed them all.
It was the same in the days of Lot: People were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building.
But on the day Lot left Sodom, fire and sulfur rained down from heaven and destroyed them all.
It will be just like that on the day the Son of Man is revealed.
On that day, let no one on the housetop come down to retrieve his possessions. Likewise, let no one in the field return for anything he has left behind.
Remember Lot's wife!
Whoever tries to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will preserve it.
I tell you, on that night two people will be in one bed: one will be taken and the other left.
Two women will be grinding grain together: one will be taken and the other left."
"Where, Lord?" they asked. Jesus answered, "Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather."

context.author: Luke, the physician and companion of Paul
context.genre: Teaching on discipleship, a healing narrative, and an end-times discourse, all on the road to Jerusalem
context.audience: The disciples (v.1, 5, 22) and the Pharisees (v.20). The healing of the ten lepers is witnessed by a mixed group in a village on the border of Samaria and Galilee.
context.setting: Verse 11 puts Jesus "between Samaria and Galilee," on the border region where Jews and Samaritans lived uneasily side by side. A group of ten lepers could include both Jews and a Samaritan, since shared suffering broke down the usual barriers. Lepers had to live apart and keep their distance, which is why they stand far off and call out (v.12-13).
context.custom: A person with leprosy had to be examined by a priest to be declared clean (Leviticus 13-14), so Jesus' command "Go, show yourselves to the priests" asks for obedience before any visible healing. Jews and Samaritans avoided each other, which gives weight to Jesus' words in verse 18 about "this foreigner." A mulberry tree had deep, tough roots, so telling it to be uprooted and planted in the sea was a picture of the impossible.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 16 warned the Pharisees about money and Scripture. Chapter 17 turns to forgiveness, faith, and thanks, then to the question of when the kingdom will come. Chapter 18 will go on to prayer and humility, and then to the final approach to Jerusalem.
context.timelineBible: The Noah and Lot comparisons (v.26-30) point back to Genesis 6-9 and 18-19, where ordinary life went on until judgment came without warning. Lot's wife (Genesis 19:26) is a warning about looking back with longing. Naaman in 2 Kings 5 is a leper cleansed through obedience, and Jesus mentions him in Luke 4:27 as a foreigner whom God healed.
context.sparkNotes: Jesus tells the disciples to avoid causing others to stumble and to forgive without limit. When they ask for more faith, He says even faith the size of a mustard seed can do the impossible, and that servants who have done their duty should not expect special thanks. On the way to Jerusalem He heals ten lepers, and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to give thanks. Then the Pharisees ask when the kingdom will come, and He answers that it is already in their midst. He warns the disciples that the Son of Man's day will come suddenly, like the flood in Noah's time and the fire in Lot's.

translation.meaning: The word originally meant the trigger of a trap, then anything that makes a person fall. Here it refers to leading others, especially the vulnerable, into sin or away from faith.

Made ritually clean. Luke uses it for all ten in verses 14 and 17 but a different word, "healed" (iaomai), for the Samaritan in verse 15, and a third idea, "made well" (sōzō, "saved"), in verse 19. All ten were cleansed, but only one is told his faith has made him whole.
The phrase can mean "within you" or "in your midst/among you." Since Jesus is speaking to Pharisees, many readers take it as "in your midst," meaning that the King Himself is standing among them.
To uncover or unveil. The coming of the Son of Man is described as a public unveiling, like lightning across the sky (v.24), not a hidden or secret event.

commentary.note: Henry says giving offense is a great sin and forgiving a great duty, and that "Christians should be of a forgiving spirit, willing to make the best of every body." On the apostles' request for more faith, he says that growth in faith is something to press for in prayer, for "the increase of our faith is what we should earnestly desire." On the unprofitable servants he writes: "God is happy without us, but we are undone without him."

On the ten lepers, Henry observes that ingratitude is common and that thanks often come from the least expected person, here a Samaritan. On the kingdom, he says it is spiritual and does not come with outward display: "The kingdom of God will not change men's outward condition, but their hearts and lives." On the warnings of Noah and Lot, he reads them as calls to watchfulness and to not clinging to what is left behind.

Gill says the image of a tree uprooted and planted in the sea shows "what great things are done by faith," even when the faith is very small. He notes of the ten lepers that "instances of gratitude are few," and that Jews regarded Samaritans as strangers. On verse 21 he reads "within you" as "an inward principle of holiness in the soul," while noting that "among you" is also possible. On Lot's wife, he reads the warning as an instruction not to look back in flight, and applies it to professing believers who turn back in distress.

overview.summary: Jesus warns against causing others to stumble and tells His disciples to forgive without limit. He heals ten lepers, and only a Samaritan returns to give thanks. Asked when the kingdom comes, He says it is already in their midst.
overview.settingLine: The border between Samaria and Galilee.

history.t: The border region mixed Jews and Samaritans, who normally kept their distance.
Many expected the kingdom with signs and force, so Jesus' answer surprised them.

customs.t: A priest had to declare a leper clean, so going to him meant trusting before healing.
Lepers had to stay away and call out "unclean," so these men stood far off.

archaeology.t: Ruins on the mountain show the Samaritans' rival place of worship.
Herod rebuilt Samaria as Sebaste, and its Roman ruins still stand.

overview.discussion: Ten were healed and only one came back to thank Him. Does gratitude matter to God, or only to us?
overview.book: The third Gospel · 24 chapters. Written as an orderly account, with Acts as its sequel.
overview.author: Luke
overview.audience: Theophilus and a broad, largely Gentile readership
